h1: Agnus hops as the high alpha bittering choice from Czechia
title: Agnus Hops: High Alpha from Czechia | Craft Beer School
desc: What Agnus hops are, why they were the first Czech high alpha variety, how to dose them for 1,000 litres and where their herbal spice fits.
teaser: Agnus is the Czech answer to high alpha bittering: strong, herbal and a little spicy.
standfirst: Agnus was the first high alpha hop bred in the Czech Republic. It lets brewers bitter big beers with far less hop matter while keeping a herbal, spicy character that sits comfortably beside Czech aroma hops.
sections: The first Czech high alpha hop

Agnus was bred at the Hop Research Institute in Žatec and registered in 2001. It was the first high alpha variety from Czech breeding, a notable step for a hop industry built around the low alpha aroma hop Saaz.

Alpha acid usually falls around 9 to 14%. The aroma is stronger than its role suggests: tasters describe it as herbal, spicy and a little resinous, with some fruit. In a beer it reads as a firm, slightly earthy bitterness rather than a neutral one. That makes it a sensible choice for brewers who want high alpha efficiency without the clean, almost blank profile of some international bittering hops.

The arithmetic is simple. For a 1,000 litre beer at 40 IBU from the 60 minute addition, at 28% utilisation:

  • Agnus at 12% alpha: 40 x 1,000 / (0.12 x 0.28 x 1,000), about 1,190 g.
  • Saaz at 3.5% alpha: 40 x 1,000 / (0.035 x 0.28 x 1,000), about 4,080 g.

Less than a third of the hop weight for the same bitterness means less leafy matter in the kettle, less wort lost with the trub and less grassy polyphenol character in the beer. For a brewery paying import duty and freight on every kilo of hops, it also means fewer kilos to ship, store cold and pay for.

Its herbal spice suits beers with enough body or hop character to carry it:

  • Czech style lagers, as the bittering hop under Saaz or other Czech aroma varieties.
  • Stronger lagers and bocks, where higher gravity lowers utilisation and a high alpha hop keeps the hop load sensible.
  • IPAs, where it supplies base bitterness under fruit forward late hops.
  • Dark beers, where roast and caramel easily absorb its earthiness.

In a very delicate beer, such as a light helles at 18 IBU, a cleaner hop may sit better. Agnus will work there, but its character can show through more than you expect.
How it compares with other high alpha hops

Against Herkules from Germany, Agnus is usually a little lower in alpha and similar in spicy character. Against Warrior or Magnum, it is less neutral, with more herbal flavour. Against Bravo or Columbus, it is less fruity and less resinous.

Its cohumulone share is relatively high, as with many older high alpha hops. Some brewers link that to a coarser bitterness, though the evidence is mixed. At normal doses most find Agnus bitterness firm rather than harsh. If you push a pale beer very high in IBU on Agnus alone, taste it against a version bittered with a lower cohumulone hop.

Utilisation is not fixed. In a stronger wort, such as a bock at an original gravity around 1.066, fewer alpha acids isomerise and stay in solution. A brewer who uses the same 28% utilisation for a 1.044 lager and a 1.066 bock will overshoot the lager or undershoot the bock.

Most brewing software adjusts for gravity, but each brewhouse is different: boil vigour, kettle shape and whirlpool time all move the real figure. The reliable fix is to send a few finished beers for IBU analysis and correct your own utilisation numbers. Understanding why the numbers move is what lets you trust them.

High alpha hops lose alpha acid in storage, faster when warm. Keep Agnus frozen at around minus 18 °C in sealed foil. In India, ask your importer how the hops were held between port and brewery, because a long, warm stretch in a warehouse can take a noticeable bite out of the alpha figure on the certificate. When in doubt, dose a pilot batch and check the IBU before you commit a full brew.

For very big beers some brewers move part of the bittering from pellets to CO2 hop extract, a resin concentrate of the alpha acids and oils. Extract adds almost no leafy matter, so kettle losses fall further. Pellets keep more of the hop's herbal character, which is part of the reason to choose Agnus in the first place.

A sensible middle path for a strong lager or IPA is to keep Agnus pellets for the main bittering charge and add extract only if the hop mass becomes a problem for your whirlpool or trub separation. Our guide to hop extracts and cryo hops covers how extract is dosed.

Take one beer you brew regularly with a lower alpha bittering hop. Recalculate the 60 minute addition with Agnus from the certificate of a lot you can buy. Brew it once at the same target IBU and compare the two beers blind. If the bitterness is clean and the herbal note is welcome, you have cut the hop weight in your kettle by a large margin.
